constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
Situations that put my body under stress

Negative Appraisals.value: I can no longer trust my own body
I have permanently changed for the worse
My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: Escape route planning implies a prominent ongoing external-danger/triggered-threat pattern in public places, but the formulation specifies no active links involving Triggers or Threat, and the rest of the profile is centered on bodily vulnerability and negative beliefs rather than situational danger. This makes the item poorly aligned with the formulation and cross-node content.

issues.item: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: Distrust of others is not impossible after a life-threatening accident, but in this profile it introduces an interpersonal/paranoid theme that is not supported by the other selected items or the formulation. The remaining items focus on bodily unreliability and permanent damage after an accident, so this item is the least coherent with the trauma-linked appraisal pattern presented.

vignette:
Amir, at seventy-five, had always understood himself through his hands. They were instruments of creation, strong and calloused from a lifetime of shaping stone and steel. Now, he mostly watched them tremble as they rested in his lap. His sprawling, light-filled studio, once the core of his world, had been silent for six months, ever since the fall. He had been working on a large marble commission, perched on a scaffold three metres up, when his foot simply slipped. There was no grand reason, no faulty board or sudden noise, just a momentary lapse in balance. He remembered the sickening weightlessness, the rush of air, and a single, clear thought: This is how it ends. The impact with the concrete floor was a brutal, shattering event that broke three ribs and his left femur. Lying there, unable to breathe for the pain, he was certain he would die alone amongst his unfinished creations.

The physical recovery was slow but steady, yet a different kind of injury had taken root. In the long, quiet afternoons, Amir found himself lost in a labyrinth of unanswerable questions. He would sit for hours, replaying the moment his foot left the scaffold, trying to understand why it happened to him, now, after a lifetime of such work. Was it a punishment? A warning? This relentless search for meaning yielded no comfort, only a deepening conviction that he had been fundamentally altered. He had come to believe that the fall wasn't just an accident but a revelation of a deeper fragility he had never acknowledged. His body, once a reliable partner in his art, now felt like a traitor. He was certain it had been permanently damaged in ways the X-rays could never show, riddled with invisible weaknesses just waiting to give way again.

This belief governed his every move. His life shrank to a cautious circuit between his armchair, the kitchen, and his bed. He began a ritual of constant self-surveillance, his hands frequently probing the healed ridge of his femur or pressing against his ribs, searching for any hint of pain or instability. A simple muscle twinge in his back could trigger an hour of quiet panic, his mind convinced it was the prelude to another catastrophic failure. He refused to lift anything heavier than a kettle, and the thought of walking on the uneven flagstones in his garden was enough to make his heart pound. The studio, with its ladders and heavy blocks of stone, became a place of profound threat. He would stand at the door, looking in at the dust gathering on his tools and the half-finished marble figure shrouded in a sheet, and feel a wave of grief and terror so intense he would have to retreat back to the safety of his living room.

The change was not lost on his daughter, Layla. She saw her once-vital father become a ghost in his own home. The breaking point came when his five-year-old grandson, Karim, ran to him, arms outstretched, shouting "Up, Jiddo, up!" Amir flinched back, shaking his head, a look of pure fear on his face. The confusion and hurt in the little boy’s eyes were more painful than any physical injury had been. It was after Layla found him weeping silently in his chair later that day that she insisted he seek help. Amir agreed, not out of hope, but from a sense of exhaustion. He has come to therapy convinced that he is a broken man, that his life as an artist and a grandfather is over. What frightens him most is the possibility that he is right, but buried deep beneath the fear is the faintest whisper of a desire: to one day feel the cool, solid reassurance of stone under his hands without the world falling away beneath him.
